source: Merton (1942/1973) Science and Democratic Social Structure: the four norms (read via a reprint page)
finding: Merton states four institutional imperatives of science: communism (findings are common property), universalism (claims judged by impersonal criteria whatever the source), disinterestedness (institutional control of motives, not saintly scientists), organised scepticism (detached empirical and logical scrutiny).
numbers: No sample or statistics. Evidence is historical cases: Newton-Leibniz priority dispute, Cavendish withholding, 1914 nationalist attacks, Nazi 'Aryan science', Soviet 1948.
quote: Truth-claims, whatever their source, are to be subjected to preestablished impersonal criteria.
limits: Conceptual essay. Norms are claimed from historical illustration, not measured. Written in the shadow of totalitarian attacks on science. Page was read through a summarising fetch, so quote is as returned.
agent_relevance: Universalism maps to blind judging (G5): strip author, institution and status before scoring. Scepticism maps to G3: test claims on what they were not fitted to.

source: Merton (1942) disinterestedness and fraud
finding: Merton explains the near absence of fraud in science by peer scrutiny, not by better personal morals. Control is structural: results are open to expert check.
numbers: Qualitative claim. The text gives no fraud rate.
limits: Claim is asserted, not measured. Later questionable-practice surveys challenge 'virtual absence of fraud'.
agent_relevance: Do not rely on the generator's honesty. Rely on an outside check the generator cannot influence (G2, G3, G5, G8).

source: Merton (1942) communism and the priority/credit exchange
finding: Scientists keep only recognition and esteem as their property claim. Open sharing is paid for with credit, which is why priority disputes are intense.
numbers: Cases: Newton-Leibniz, Cavendish; patents by Einstein, Millikan, Compton, Langmuir cited as efforts to keep work public.
limits: Interpretive. Later work (Strevens) turns this credit exchange into a formal incentive model.
agent_relevance: Shared findings only help if read by independent checkers. A single agent has no community, so communism becomes: keep an open, checkable record of every attempt and failure.

source: Mitroff (1974) Norms and counter-norms in a select group of the Apollo moon scientists, Am. Sociol. Rev. 39(4):579-595
finding: Study of prominent Apollo lunar-sample scientists found each Mertonian norm has an opposed counter-norm that scientists also endorse: solitariness (secrecy) vs communism, particularism vs universalism, interestedness vs disinterestedness, organised dogmatism vs organised scepticism. Mitroff argued science runs on ambivalence between both sets.
numbers: 42 prominent scientists, studied over about 3.5 years (from a search-result summary; full paper not opened).
limits: Not opened. Only a search summary and secondary sources (Wikipedia, Anderson 2010) were read. Small elite single-field sample; interview data. Per-norm percentages not seen.
agent_relevance: Counter-norms are not only bugs. Organised dogmatism (defend your own theory) can be useful early. Warns against a schema that forces doubt on a schedule (G1).

source: Wikipedia: Mertonian norms (secondary summary of counter-norms)
finding: Lists Mitroff's pairs: secrecy vs communality, particularism vs universalism, self-interestedness vs disinterestedness, organised dogmatism vs organised scepticism. Notes Ziman renamed communism as communalism, and that Anderson 2010 and Macfarlane and Cheng 2008 extended or re-examined the norms.
numbers: No numbers on the page.
limits: Encyclopedia page, used only to confirm naming. Not primary. Macfarlane and Cheng 2008 not opened.
agent_relevance: Naming reference only.

source: Anderson, Ronning, DeVries, Martinson (2010) Extending the Mertonian Norms: Scientists' Subscription to Norms of Research, J. Higher Educ. 81(3):366-393
finding: Scientists strongly endorse Mertonian norms and mostly reject the original counter-norms, but endorse some new ones (employment, narrowness). The survey measured subscription (what should be), not behaviour.
numbers: 6 focus groups, 51 scientists, 3 universities. National survey: 3,600 mid-career NIH R01 grantees (52% response) and 4,160 early-career postdocs (43%). Mertonian norms endorsed 73% to 91% (quality 91%, governance 80%, breadth 68% and 72%). Original counter-norms 18% to 23%, except self-interestedness 33% mid-career and 25% early-career. Employment and narrowness counter-norms 44% to 65%.
limits: Self-report of what should hold, US biomedical only, response rates 43-52%. Not a behaviour measure.
agent_relevance: Norm subscription is high but says little about conduct. Same gap as a model that states a rule yet breaks it. Check behaviour in code, not the model's stated commitment.

source: Anderson et al. (2010): career-stage differences
finding: Early-career scientists endorse organised scepticism, employment and breadth more, and particularism, self-interestedness, quantity, calling and narrowness less than mid-career scientists.
numbers: Same samples (3,600 mid-career, 4,160 early-career). Per-item gaps are in Figure 1 of the paper, not in the text opened.
limits: Cross-sectional, so cohort and career-stage effects cannot be separated.
agent_relevance: Weak. Suggests norms are learned and context-bound, so a scaffold must state them operationally.

source: Anderson, Martinson, De Vries (2007) Normative dissonance in science: results from a national survey of U.S. scientists, J. Empir. Res. Hum. Res. Ethics 2(4):3-14
finding: Record located (PMID 19385804, not in PMC). From memory of the literature: a national survey of US funded scientists found a gap between norms they subscribe to and behaviour they see in colleagues, called normative dissonance.
numbers: Numbers not read. Do not cite figures from this line.
limits: Abstract and full text not opened this session.
agent_relevance: Same lesson as a06: stated norm and observed practice diverge.

source: Merton (1968) The Matthew effect in science, Science 159:56-63 (seen through Huber et al. 2022 and Wikipedia)
finding: Eminent scientists get disproportionately great credit for the same work; unknown scientists get disproportionately little. This is a measured breach of universalism.
numbers: Wikipedia gives no Nobel-credit numbers. A later citation: researchers just above a funding threshold got more than twice the funding over 8 years than near-identical scorers just below (Bol et al. 2018, Netherlands).
quote: eminent scientists get disproportionately great credit for their contribution to science
limits: Original paper not opened; quote came through Huber et al. Funding result is secondary.
agent_relevance: Status is a cue that should not enter a score. Remove it before judging (G5).

source: Huber, Inoua, Kerschbamer, Konig-Kersting, Palan, Smith (2022) Nobel and novice: author prominence affects peer review, PNAS 119(41)
finding: Preregistered field experiment. The same finance paper, by a Nobel laureate and an early-career associate, was sent to reviewers with the laureate's name, the junior name, or no name. Status changed both willingness to review and the verdict.
numbers: 3,299 invitations, 2,611 replies. Invitation accepted: 28.52% (junior shown), 30.74% (anonymous), 38.54% (laureate shown); anonymous vs laureate p=0.0031. Recommend reject: 23% (laureate), 48% (anonymous), 65% (junior). Over 20% recommended accept with the laureate, under 2% with the junior. Second source (Pataranutaporn 2025) quotes 22.6/48.2/65.4 from about 3,300 reviewers.
limits: One paper, one field (finance), one journal. Name origin and race could not be held constant between the two authors. Low stakes (50 USD token).
agent_relevance: Strongest human evidence that universalism fails in practice. A verdict moves by tens of points from the name alone. Justifies blind judges (G5).

source: Tomkins, Zhang, Heavlin (2017) Single versus double blind reviewing at WSDM 2017 (PNAS version: Reviewer bias in single- versus double-blind peer review)
finding: Controlled experiment: each paper had four reviewers, two who saw author names and two who did not. Single-blind reviewers favoured famous authors and top institutions.
numbers: Odds multipliers for recommending acceptance: 1.63 famous author, 1.58 top university (p=0.012), 2.10 top company (p=0.002). Female authors: odds 0.78, not significant. Equivalent to quality shifts of 0.57 to 0.92 standard deviations. Single-blind reviewers bid for 22% fewer papers and preferred top institutions.
limits: Single computer-science conference. Female effect underpowered. The paper's meta-analysis places the effects in line with other experiments.
agent_relevance: Direct numbers for how much author cues move a human judge. Use as the target size when testing our own judge for the same leak.

source: Blank (1991) The effects of double-blind versus single-blind reviewing, Am. Econ. Rev. 81:1041-1067 (as described in Pataranutaporn 2025 and Tomkins 2017)
finding: Controlled study of papers submitted to the American Economic Review 1987-1989, double-blind vs single-blind reviewers. Cited as the classic test of institutional and status bias.
numbers: Numbers not read this session.
limits: Not opened. Secondary descriptions only.
agent_relevance: Background.

source: Peters and Ceci (1982) Peer-review practices of psychological journals: the fate of published articles, submitted again
finding: From memory: 12 previously published papers were resubmitted with changed author names and institutions to the journals that had published them. Most were rejected, mostly for methodological flaws.
numbers: Counts not verified this session; do not cite.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Another demonstration that status cues and scepticism interact.

source: Strevens (2003) The role of the priority rule in science, J. Philosophy 100:55-79
finding: From memory: formal model in which a winner-take-all credit rule pushes selfish scientists to spread effort across rival research programmes in a way that can match the social optimum. It gives a computational account of why communism plus credit works.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Not opened. PDF fetch was refused. Summary from memory.
agent_relevance: Diversity of approaches inside a system helps, but G4 warns that samples from one model are not independent.

source: Kitcher (1990) The division of cognitive labor, J. Philosophy 87:5-22
finding: From memory: formal model of how a community should split effort between rival methods. Self-interested credit-seeking can give a better split than everyone following the single best-looking method.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Same caution: diversity needs real independence, not repeated draws of one model.

source: Liang, Zhang, Cao et al. (2023) Can large language models provide useful feedback on research papers? A large-scale empirical analysis
finding: GPT-4 reviews of full papers overlap with human reviews about as much as two humans overlap with each other. Researchers rated the feedback helpful.
numbers: 3,096 papers from 15 Nature-family journals and 1,709 ICLR papers. Overlap of GPT-4 with human: 30.85% (Nature), 39.23% (ICLR). Human-human overlap: 28.58% and 35.25%. User study: 308 researchers at 110 US institutions; 57.4% found it helpful or very helpful; 82.4% found it more useful than at least some human reviews.
limits: Overlap is of comment points, not of verdicts. Overlap was higher for weaker papers.
agent_relevance: An LLM can play organised sceptic at human-reviewer level on surface points. Its scepticism is cheap, so use it to generate objections that code then checks.

source: Liang, Izzo, Zhang et al. (2024) Monitoring AI-modified content at scale: ChatGPT in AI conference peer reviews
finding: Between 6.5% and 16.9% of peer-review text at ICLR 2024, NeurIPS 2023, CoRL 2023 and EMNLP 2023 was likely substantially modified by an LLM. Rates were higher in reviews with lower confidence, near the deadline, and from reviewers who answered rebuttals less.
numbers: Range 6.5% to 16.9% across the four venues; corpus-level maximum likelihood estimate, not per-review detection.
limits: Corpus-level estimate. Assumes the reference texts represent human and AI text.
agent_relevance: The community's scepticism is now partly produced by models. Low effort plus LLM means weaker independence between reviewers.

source: Latona, Ribeiro, Davidson, Veselovsky, West (2024) The AI Review Lottery
finding: At ICLR 2024 reviews flagged as AI-assisted scored papers higher than other reviews of the same paper, and raised the acceptance chance for borderline papers.
numbers: At least 15.8% of ICLR 2024 reviews AI-assisted (GPTZero). In 53.4% of different-score review pairs the AI-assisted review scored higher (p=0.002). Relative +14.4%. Borderline papers with an AI-assisted review were 4.9 points more likely to be accepted (p=0.024).
limits: Quasi-experiment on observed data. The detector is imperfect and gives a lower bound. Reviewer type may confound.
agent_relevance: LLM judges lean lenient. Do not let an LLM both draft and grade; calibrate score inflation in code (G5).

source: Ye, Pang, Chai et al. (2024) Are we there yet? Revealing the risks of utilizing large language models in scholarly peer review
finding: LLM reviewers can be steered by hidden text in the paper, are swayed by disclosed minor limitations, prefer longer papers, and give better scores when famous names or institutions are attached.
numbers: ICLR 2024 data. Explicit manipulation: agreement with the injected content about 90% (92.49% after manipulation); agreement with human reviews fell from 53% to 16%; mean rating rose from 5.34 to 7.99. Simulation: manipulating 5% of reviews pushes 12% of papers out of the top 30%. Implicit manipulation: LLM reviews 4.5 times more consistent with author-disclosed limitations than human reviews. Authorship test on 500 papers: share rated 6 or higher rose from 36.8% to 40.8% (famous university), 41.6% (company), 41.2% (well-known researcher). Title-only papers scored at or above 42% of full papers.
limits: The rating model is itself an LLM. Authorship swap tested on one review system. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Direct LLM-side counter-universalism: prestige leaks into scores. Also shows a judge is attackable by text, so judge input must be sanitised in code.

source: Pataranutaporn, Powdthavee, Achiwaranguprok, Maes (2025) Can AI solve the peer review crisis? Experiments on 1,000+ economics papers
finding: Four LLMs (GPT-4o, Claude 3.5, Gemma 3, LLaMA 3.3) rank anonymised economics papers in line with journal prestige, but three of four rate the same paper higher when it carries a top male author or an elite affiliation.
numbers: Experiment 1: over 29,000 evaluations of 1,220 papers from 110 journals. Experiment 2: 8,910 evaluations on 330 papers. GPT rated top male authors +0.39 points (SE 0.042) over anonymous, larger than the gap between a journal ranked 51-75 and one ranked 1-25. Top female authors rated below top male authors (p<0.01 for GPT, Gemma, LLaMA); random names equal to blind. MIT and Harvard raised ratings for all four LLMs; Claude was the exception for author prominence but penalised one Thai university.
limits: Journals chosen outside training data, but memorisation cannot be fully excluded. Ratings are ordinal LLM outputs.
agent_relevance: Largest LLM replication of status bias. Confirms the blind-judge rule and shows model-specific differences, so test the exact judge we use.

source: Prestige over merit: an adapted audit of LLM bias in peer review (2025)
finding: GPT-4o-mini in editor and reviewer roles gave slightly better quality scores and fewer reject recommendations when author identity was shown. Low-prestige institutions were penalised a little. Gender and race effects were mostly not significant.
numbers: 10 PNAS papers, 40 synthetic names, 4 institutions (2 R1, 2 R2) plus a blinded control, 50 runs per profile, about 400,500 outputs. Identity shown: reviewer reject 6.7% to 5.0% (-1.7 pp, about -25% relative); editor quality +2.4%; reviewer quality +1.0%. Low prestige vs R1: reviewer reject 6.7% to 7.2% (+0.5 pp), concentrated in biology (+0.016). Editor desk reject unchanged (about 10%). Gender n.s.
limits: Only 10 papers, one model. The model recognised 6 of 10 authors until titles were edited. Count inconsistencies in the paper (80,000 vs 80,500). Effects are small, so this partly disagrees with a19 and a20.
agent_relevance: Counter-evidence on effect size: the leak exists but may be small for some models. Measure ours, do not assume.

source: Jin et al. (2024) AgentReview: exploring peer review dynamics with LLM agents
finding: LLM agents playing reviewers, authors and area chairs reproduce known sociological effects: social conformity, altruism fatigue, groupthink, authority bias and anchoring.
numbers: More than 53,800 generated documents, over 10,000 reviews, 500+ ICLR submissions. Conformity after rebuttal cuts rating spread by 27.2%. One irresponsible reviewer lowers commitment of all reviewers by 18.7%. Biased reviewers amplify each other: 0.17 rating drop among biased and 0.25 among unbiased reviewers. If reviewers know author identity for only 10% of papers, decisions change by 27.7%. 37.1% of decisions change with just one biased reviewer; 30.6% change when area chairs rely on their own judgment.
limits: Simulated agents, not real people. Validity is checked only against sociological theory, not against real decisions.
agent_relevance: A committee of copies of one model reproduces conformity and authority bias. Supports G4 and G5: show a judge no majority and no author; judge independently.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs generate novel research ideas? A large-scale human study with 100+ NLP researchers
finding: In a blind, style-normalised review, experts judged LLM-generated research ideas more novel than expert ideas, slightly weaker on feasibility. LLM self-evaluation failed and generated ideas lacked diversity.
numbers: 79 expert reviewers; 49 ideas per condition. Novelty mean: human 4.84 (SD 1.79, 119 reviews), AI 5.64 (SD 1.76, 109), AI plus human rerank 5.81 (SD 1.66, 109); Welch t-test with Bonferroni p<0.01. Overall score: human 4.68, AI 4.85 (n.s.), rerank 5.34 (p=0.04). Only about 5% of seed ideas were non-duplicates after dedup at cosine 0.8. After style normalisation, expert judges told AI from human ideas at 50% accuracy.
limits: Novelty is judged, not run (G8); the paper says experts judge novelty poorly. Execution of ideas was proposed, not part of this result.
agent_relevance: A blind, style-normalised judge is a working form of universalism. The same paper shows why model self-ranking of ideas cannot be the final selector (G8).

source: Beel et al. (2025) Evaluating Sakana's AI Scientist for autonomous research: wishful thinking or an emerging reality?
finding: An independent evaluation of an automated science pipeline found weak scepticism: poor novelty checks, many failed experiments, thin literature.
numbers: 5 of 12 experiments (42%) failed from coding errors. Each code iteration adds only about 8% more characters. Median 5 citations per paper; only 5 of 34 citations from 2020 or later. Well-known ideas such as micro-batching for SGD were labelled novel.
limits: Small number of runs on the first version of the system. Later versions (AI Scientist v2) may differ.
agent_relevance: Without an outside check, an agent's own novelty claim is cheap. Supports G8 and the need for organised scepticism with a real search.

source: Panickssery, Bowman, Feng (2024) LLM evaluators recognize and favor their own generations
finding: LLM judges score their own outputs higher. Self-recognition rises with self-preference, and the two are linearly related.
numbers: GPT-4 identifies its own text among itself, another LLM and a human with 73.5% accuracy out of the box. GPT-3.5 and Llama 2 reach over 90% self-recognition after fine-tuning on 500 examples. Self-recognition and self-preference are linearly correlated in fine-tuning experiments.
limits: Summarisation tasks (CNN/DailyMail, XSum). Causality shown by fine-tuning, not natural variation.
agent_relevance: LLM version of failed disinterestedness. A model must not judge its own text; hide authorship from the judge (G5).

source: Wang, Li, Chen et al. (2023) Large language models are not fair evaluators
finding: The order in which two responses appear flips the LLM referee's winner. Averaging over both orders reduces this.
numbers: With ChatGPT as evaluator, Vicuna-13B beat ChatGPT on 66 of 80 queries just by reordering the answers.
limits: One query set of 80 prompts. Calibration still leaves some bias.
agent_relevance: Positional particularism. Randomise and double-order candidates in code (G5).

source: Zheng, Chiang, Sheng et al. (2023) Judging LLM-as-a-judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena
finding: Strong LLM judges agree with humans above 80%, the same as humans agree with each other, but show position, verbosity and self-enhancement bias.
numbers: GPT-4 agreement above 80% on 3K expert votes and 3K crowd votes. Position consistency: GPT-4 65.0% (default), GPT-3.5 46.2%, Claude-v1 23.8%; few-shot raised GPT-4 to 77.5%. Repetitive-list attack failure rate: Claude-v1 91.3%, GPT-3.5 91.3%, GPT-4 8.7%. Math grading failures on 10 questions (20 trials): 14/20 default, 6/20 chain-of-thought, 3/20 with a reference answer.
limits: Only 10 math questions in the grading test. Biases are lower for GPT-4 but not absent.
agent_relevance: A reference answer or code-checked fact cuts judge error most. Matches G2 and G3: judge against real output.

source: Thakkar, Yuksekgonul, Silberg et al. (2025) Can LLM feedback enhance review quality? A randomized study of 20K reviews at ICLR 2025
finding: A randomised trial gave LLM feedback on vague or unprofessional review comments. Reviewers updated, and reviews got longer and more informative.
numbers: Over 20,000 randomly chosen reviews. 27% of reviewers who got feedback updated their review; over 12,000 suggestions were incorporated; average +80 words among updaters. Feedback was sent only if it passed automated reliability tests.
limits: Quality judged by blinded researchers. Longer is not always better; verbosity may itself be a bias.
agent_relevance: LLM as a gate before review output, with reliability tests as code guardrails. Fits the schema split: the model proposes, code gates.
